newsitem.title: TURKEY: High Turkish growth rate to slow gradually - OECD.
newsitem.headline: High Turkish growth rate to slow gradually - OECD.

text.p: Turkey's growth rate is expected to slow gradually from current high levels as a result of fiscal tightening and longer debt maturities, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said.

"The OECD Secretariat projects that economic growth will gradually slow in response to a slight fiscal tightening and some lengthening in the average maturity of the debt," the OECD said in its twice yearly economic outlook.
It forecast that GDP growth will decline from a 10 percent year-on-year rise in the first half of 1996 to a projected 7.5 percent in 1996 as a whole, to 5.75 percent in 1997 and 5.0 percent in 1998.
The OECD said the economic situation in Turkey remains difficult. Macroeconomic imbalances have worsened and financial market uncertainty remains pronounced.
Fiscal policy has been expansionary and monetary policy is accommodating inflation of some 80 percent, it said.
The public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR), estimated to have risen sharply to 10 percent of GDP in 1996, must be improved "to maintain a measure of financial market confidence", the report said.

"Otherwise, the Treasury's difficulties in managing the public debt could be exacerbated, leading to accelerating inflation, pressure on the exchange rate and eventually to a sharp drop in output," it said.
The PSBR will only decline slowly to some six percent of GDP by 1998, the OECD forecast. It said this situation largely reflects extraordinarily high nominal and real interest rates.
The government has programmed a zero PSBR in its draft 1997 budget.
The organisation said it assumed privatisation revenues amounting to five percent of GDP that are programmed into the budget for 1997 will take longer to be realised.
It said inflation is projected to decline modestly to around 65 percent in 1998 and the current account deficit to widen to around 4 percent of GDP in 1998 from 2.9 percent expected in 1996.
"The risks and uncertainties surrounding these projections are large. The new government's resolve to address the economy's fundamental problems has yet to be tested," the OECD said.
But it said concrete measures to achieve a medium-term improvement in the fiscal position "could quickly lead to a virtuous circle of falling inflation and lower interest payments."
